name: Tongkat ali (Eurycoma longifolia)
short: Case reports: liver injury with jaundice; new atrial flutter. Product tests: mercury or lead above limits; signs of a sildenafil-like drug in 2 of 10. Lowered propranolol levels in volunteers.
text: Serious harms (case reports, by mouth): a 47-year-old man developed yellowing of the eyes and skin and raised liver enzymes shortly after starting tongkat ali, was admitted to hospital and improved after stopping it; the authors excluded other causes and call it the first reported case of its kind. A 71-year-old man developed new atrial flutter (an abnormal heart rhythm) after starting tongkat ali; other causes were ruled out, and the authors presume the supplement caused it. Contamination (laboratory tests of products, not reports of harm in people): in a 2004 analysis of 100 Malaysian products of a herbal preparation containing tongkat ali (the abstract does not give the Latin name), 36% contained 0.52 to 5.30 ppm of mercury and did not meet the national quality requirement for traditional medicines. In a 2003 analysis of 100 Malaysian products of a herbal preparation, 8 contained 10.64 to 20.72 ppm of lead and did not meet the same requirement; the abstract identifies these 8 only by product names that include tongkat ali or Eurycoma. In both analyses the authors say products that complied cannot be assumed free of contamination because of batch-to-batch inconsistency. A laboratory screening of ten commercial products containing E. longifolia found spectra suggesting a sildenafil analogue (a drug of the same type as a prescription erectile dysfunction medicine) in two products bought online. A DNA-barcoding study of E. longifolia herbal medicinal products found 37% of the tested products authentic and 27% adulterated; the abstract does not give the number of products or what the adulterated products contained. Trials (root water extracts by mouth): in a 4-week placebo-controlled trial in middle-aged Japanese adults (83 completed and 81 were analysed), no severe adverse events were observed; in a 12-week placebo-controlled trial in 109 men aged 30 to 55, all safety parameters were comparable to placebo (the abstract does not list adverse events); in a 24-week trial of tongkat ali combined with multivitamins in 93 adults, 13 adverse events were reported, seven with the combination and six with placebo. Interactions: in a placebo-controlled crossover study in 14 healthy young men (not people with erectile dysfunction), a water-based extract taken with a single dose of propranolol, a blood pressure medicine, lowered propranolol's bioavailability by 29% and its peak level by 42%; propranolol's effect on the body was not changed in these volunteers, but the authors advise caution when the two are taken together and note that users of the herb may include people with high blood pressure who take propranolol. In laboratory tests with human liver microsomes and enzymes, a root extract weakly inhibited CYP1A2, CYP2A6 and CYP2C19, enzymes that break down many medicines; this is a laboratory result, not a human interaction study.
